topic: Prompting basics from Anthropic's own guidance: why Claude's answers come back generic, five rules that matter, and one reusable prompt template
audience: Professionals who use Claude (or any AI chat) at work and get answers that are bland, generic or confidently wrong
goal: Write prompts with a goal, context, a picture of good and room for doubt, using one template they keep and reuse, and save their standing rules once in Instructions
notes: Anthropic's prompting guide says to treat Claude like a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows: the more precisely you explain what you want, the better the result. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Anthropic's 'key test' for a prompt: show it to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it; if they would be confused, Claude will be too. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Be specific about the output format and constraints, give steps as numbered or bulleted lists when order or completeness matters, and if you want more than the minimum, ask for it explicitly. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Give the reason behind an instruction: Anthropic's example replaces 'NEVER use ellipses' with an explanation that the reply will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, because Claude can generalize from the explanation. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Anthropic calls examples (few-shot or multishot prompting) one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure, and recommends 3-5 relevant, diverse examples wrapped in <example> tags. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

Anthropic's article for Claude app users (10 Nov 2025) advises starting with one example and adding more only if the output still doesn't match, noting that Claude 4.x and similar models pay very close attention to details in examples. [https://claude.com/resources/articles/best-practices-for-prompt-engineering]

The claude.com article for app users says XML tags and heavy role prompting are less necessary with modern models: for most uses, clear headings, whitespace and explicit language work just as well, while tags still help with very complex prompts. [https://claude.com/resources/articles/best-practices-for-prompt-engineering]

Setting a role focuses Claude's behavior and tone for your use case; Anthropic says even a single sentence makes a difference. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

With long inputs (20k+ tokens), put the documents near the top of the prompt and the question at the end; Anthropic says queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30% in tests. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

To control formatting, tell Claude what to do rather than what not to do (for example, ask for 'smoothly flowing prose paragraphs' instead of saying 'Do not use markdown'), and match your prompt's own style to the output you want. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices]

To reduce hallucinations, explicitly give Claude permission to say 'I don't know'; Anthropic says this can drastically reduce false information. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations]

For long documents, ask Claude to extract word-for-word quotes first and base its answer on them, and to back each claim with a supporting quote or retract it; Anthropic says these techniques reduce but do not eliminate hallucinations. [https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations]

Anthropic's claude.com prompting article warns against over-engineering: longer, more complex prompts are not always better, the first prompt rarely works perfectly, and you should test and refine. [https://claude.com/resources/articles/best-practices-for-prompt-engineering]

Claude can 'hallucinate' incorrect or misleading information; Anthropic says not to rely on it as a singular source of truth and to scrutinize high-stakes advice and check cited sources. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8525154-claude-is-providing-incorrect-or-misleading-responses-what-s-going-on]

Account-wide Instructions are set in Settings > Your Claude > Instructions and apply to all conversations; project instructions apply within a project. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10185728-understanding-claude-s-personalization-features]

Searching past chats is available on paid plans and can be switched off at Settings > Your Claude > 'Search and reference chats'. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11817273-use-claude-s-chat-search-and-memory-to-build-on-previous-context]

Anthropic's usage tips: plan conversations (combine related questions in one message, give background up front), be specific and concise, batch similar requests into one message, and review your prompt before sending to avoid follow-ups. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9797557-usage-limit-best-practices]

To change effort in the Claude apps, click the model name next to the send button, click 'Effort', then choose a level; Low and Medium suit routine tasks and stretch usage further, while higher effort uses more tokens. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8664678-change-the-model-effort-and-thinking-settings]

Anthropic says Opus 5.5 communicates more naturally: clearer writing, the most important information up front, less jargon, and it follows the writing rules you give it. [https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5]
